Discussion

Humans need to calibrate behavioral variability to adapt to the unique demands of different environments. Across three experiments, we demonstrate that humans increase behavioral variability as they move from stable to volatile to adversarial environments, and that this increase is supported by distinct cognitive mechanisms. Modest variability demands in volatile environments are met by adjustments in learning rates and decision noise; in contrast, adversarial environments, which demand strategic unpredictability, elicit a shift towards even more decision noise and memory-based decision processes. These findings suggest that adaptive variability is not a unitary process, but a multifaceted phenomenon supported by a flexible repertoire of diverse cognitive mechanisms.

The functional importance of this adaptive variability lies primarily in its immediate strategic use. In adversarial contexts, ranging from predator-prey interactions (2) to high-stakes games and sports (1), maintaining high unpredictability (and thus high variability) is a fundamental requirement for survival and success. A predictable agent is an exploitable agent. Our findings suggest that humans address these demands for variability by transitioning toward memory-based and stochastic processes that ensure strategic unpredictability. By providing a computational account of these shifts, we offer a framework for understanding how individuals deceive opponents and generate creative variations necessary to beat adversarial environments. While the goal to try and deceive opponents is sometimes studied through the lens of Theory of Mind (the ability or attempt to infer another person's thoughts, beliefs and/or reasonings (24-26)), our results further demonstrate that humans can deploy sophisticated, unpredictable strategies through fundamental cognitive mechanisms that do not strictly require high-level social reasoning. Down the line, generating such variability in behavior is also thought to have benefits when learning a new skill, as shown in motor domains (27, 28), verbal domains (27) and cognitive domains (29, 30). In a similar vein, it has been shown that adversarial reinforcement schedules can improve learning in humans (21) and rats (31, 32). Moreover, variability is believed to push behavior outside prior limits leading to potential progress (7, 33). More broadly, these processes are thought to be important drivers for everyday learning, individual development and evolution (34) (35) (36). For these reasons, it becomes important to understand adaptive variability at a cognitive level, for which our models and their application to adversarial environments offer exciting, new possibilities (23).

A key contribution of our study is the explicit, formal comparison between volatile and adversarial environments. Prior studies have shown that volatility in reward contingencies increase variability by increasing learning rates and stochasticity, thereby facilitating rapid adaptation to changing contingencies (13, 19). Our results replicate this pattern: learning rate primarily differentiated stable from volatile environments. However, learning rates were not further increased in adversarial environments. Instead, the increased variability in adversarial environments was primarily supported by increased stochastic and memory-based mechanisms.

Participants showed higher levels of stochasticity, consistent with the idea of a stochastic generator mechanism that allows choices to be made independently of past choices (3, 4). Similarly, De Souza Barba (2015) argued that, when subjected to an adversarial environment where no actions are consistently rewarded, humans eventually switch to a default setting of 'spontaneous' behavior, resulting in highly variable sequences (37). Model fits further revealed systematic contributions of memory-based mechanisms, including action-frequency-based memory, whereby infrequent individual actions are upvalued, and episodic memory, whereby recently chosen individual actions are remembered but actively avoided. Together, these allow agents to track and counteract regularities in their own behavior to increase variability. In a similar vein, memory processes are also assumed to be involved in random number generation tasks (38) where people are instructed to generate a random sequence and optimal performance is attributed to executive functions, working memory, and inhibition (39) (40) (41) (42) (43) (44). It is possible that these memory processes rely on a unique human ability, as an earlier study modelling humans, pigeons, and rats in adversarial environments demonstrated that only humans upvalued infrequent actions when variability is required (23).

Interestingly, we further showed that participants tend to repeat rather than avoid previous action sequences more in adversarial environments (compared to volatile environments), despite being inefficient. This may reflect a human tendency to look for or favor patterns unknowingly (45) or knowingly (46), even when counterproductive (47). For example, Shani-Narkiss et al (2025), showed that humans tend to value regularities more, even when regularities do not contain any additional value. They further argued that decision making models solely resting on reward learning might be insufficient, offering further motivation to include our three memory-based parameters in a classic reinforcement learning model. Alternatively, the tendency to repeat action sequences more than to vary them may have been a strategy to try and meet first-order entropy demands. That is, to produce as many different responses as possible, participants may have cycled through the different options in a somewhat predictable manner.

Our paradigm can be leveraged to create a new window on the neural signatures of the cognitive processes that underlie adaptive variable decision-making. Understanding adaptive variability on both a behavioral and neural level will provide insights into learning and decision making (48) (49) (50). Moreover, through disentangling these different processes, we may better understand individual differences in the generation of adaptively variable behavior and cognitive flexibility more broadly (16, (51) (52) (53) (54). For example, taking apart the cognitive processes that underlie variable behavior becomes important when trying to understand neurological conditions characterized by difficulties with variability such as autism spectrum disorder. While children with autism can learn to be adaptively variable (e.g., (55), specific impairments of cognitive flexibility (56) or problems with invariance (57) could be characterized by different cognitive mechanisms.

Taken together, these findings indicate that humans have several ways of producing variable behavior to adapt to different environmental demands. Our result underscores the importance of considering adaptive variability not merely as upregulating noise, but as an adaptive resource that can be generated through multiple cognitive mechanisms.

Materials and methods

General procedure

Our paradigm is a multi-armed bandit based on a game of hide-and-seek and was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at Ghent University. Participants see a garden with several hiding spots (the bandits, see Figure 1), and must search for one of three different animal species per block: a bunny, a fox, or a cat. On each trial, participants must click on a hiding spot and are either "rewarded" with finding the animal or notified the animal is not there (indicated by a red cross; see Figure 1). Importantly, the three animals have different "hiding" strategies requiring different optimal variability levels in participants' choices. Different animal types were counterbalanced across participants over different hiding strategies.

One of the animal species is a stable hider, meaning this animal can be found behind some hiding spot(s) with a high probability and behind the other hiding spots with a low probability. A second animal species is a volatile hider, meaning that the high probable hiding spot(s) changed on average every 15 trials (change point sampled from a discretized normal distribution Ν(15,3)).

The third animal is an adversarial hider, meaning that its hiding spots were chosen as a function of participants' previous choices to maximize variability (4, 58). Namely, we tracked frequencies of participants' response sequences and if it was among the least frequent occurring subsequences, the animal was found, otherwise it was not. Irrespective of the outcome, the frequency of the current subsequence was updated by adding 1 to its frequency. All other frequencies were subtracted by 1/63. Finally, all frequencies were multiplied by φ = 0.984, serving as an amnesia coefficient to account for recency (see also (59). The order in which the different animals were presented was randomized. The exact reward probabilities and length of sequences that were tracked, varied across experiments (see below).

Figure 1 shows the structure of an experiment with 8 or 4 hiding spots and 200 trials per block (sequences of length 200). The experiments always started by agreeing with an informed consent form, after which participants were asked about their gender, handedness, English proficiency level, and age. Next, participants received instructions on how to play. They were instructed that multiple animals of the same species could be hidden at the same time, but that they could only click one hiding spot at a time. This was to counteract default expectations about the chance level of finding an animal, which was generally higher than 1/(number of hiding spots) in our experiment. We also told participants that different animals may have different hiding strategies, and that animals could stay at the same location or change locations, irrespective of whether the previous trial was successful or not. After these instructions, there was a practice block of 10 trials where participants had to search for a panda. If something was unclear, participants could scroll through the instructions again after this practice block. Before the start of each block, participants first saw which animal they had to search for. After clicking 'Start', they could continuously click on hiding spots without a response deadline for a maximum number of trials (defined per experiment). After each block, they saw their total score for that block. At the end of the experiment, we asked participants if they noticed what the different hiding strategies of the animals were and if they themselves applied different searching strategies. The experimental code is publicly available at https://github.com/jareynde/HideAndSeek.

Experiment 1

Sixty-eight participants participated in Experiment 1 (18.8 +/-2 years, 63 female, 4 male and 1 non-binary). This experiment consisted of 2400 trials that were divided over 12 blocks of 200 trials each. In each block, only one type of animal could be found. The order of the three conditions was randomized for the first three blocks and repeated four times (all participants searched for each animal 800 times). There were eight hiding spots. The stable animal could be found behind three hiding spots with a 70% probability and behind the other hiding spots with a 30% probability. These probabilities remained associated to the same hiding spots for the entire stable block duration. The volatile animal could be found behind three hiding spots with a probability of 90%, and behind the other hiding spots with a probability of 10%, but these probabilities shuffled among hiding spots every ~15 trials to indicate a change of underlying environmental structure. The adversarial animal could only be found if a sequence of two responses (a response pair) was among the 60% least occurring in that participants' entire choice history. Frequencies were reset every block.

Experiment 2

There were 150 participants in Experiment 2 (18.3 +/-1.6 years, 132 female, 18 male). Like Experiment 1, there were 2400 trials in total, but now divided over three blocks of 800 trials each. Participants received a small break after every 200 trials where they saw their intermediate score. The hiding probabilities in the stable context remained the same for the entire block duration and the frequencies of choice pairs in the adversarial context were not reset throughout the entire 800 adversarial trials. Again, only one animal type could be found per block. All participants searched for each animal 800 times, and the order of blocks was randomized. There were eight hiding spots in total, and the reward probabilities were the same as for Experiment 1.

Experiment 3

In Experiment 3, 72 people participated (18.5 +/-0.8 years, 63 female, 8 male and 1 other).

Like Experiment 2, this experiment consisted of three blocks of 800 trials each, with one animal randomly assigned per block. Unlike the previous two experiments, there were four hiding spots, not eight. In the stable environment, there was one hiding spot with a fixed probability of 70% to find the animal (the other three had a fixed probability of 10%). In the volatile environment, there was one hiding spot with an 85% probability of finding the animal, where the other three had a probability of 5%. These reward probabilities were again shuffled every +/-15 trials. Last, in the adversarial environment, the animal could only be found if a sequence of three consecutive responses (a response triplet) occurred among the 60% of the least frequent response triplets in the choice history of that participant.

Behavioral analyses

To evaluate the variability in choice sequences, we calculated second-order entropy scores, a normalized form of Shannon entropy (60). Entropy is a highly used measure for uncertainty and information in a sequence (60, 61) and is traditionally used to represent the variability of sequences in adversarial environments (3, 4). The classic Shannon entropy is divided by log 2 (𝑥) with x the total number of options or alternatives. This normalizes the entropy score between 0 and 1, where 0 means low variability and 1 means high variability. It is calculated as follows: where

Here, 𝑈 2 indicates the second order entropy and 𝑈 1 is the first-order entropy. The (normalized) first order entropy calculates a weighted probability of the occurrence of each of the possible response options or actions, where n represents the total number of possible actions and p1,i represents the probability of occurrence for each action i. The (normalized) second-order entropy computes a weighted probability of the presence of each of the possible pairs of response options or actions in the sequence, where m represents the total number of possible pairs (m = n 2 ) and p2,k represents the probability that response pair k is present in the sequence. The (normalized) second-order entropy scores are generally lower for shorter sequences with the same number of options, and higher for sequences with equal length but less choice options. Therefore, we further standardized the (normalized) second-order entropy by dividing it by a baseline for each experiment separately: 𝑈 2,𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑎𝑟𝑑 = 𝑈 2 𝑈 2,𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 where 𝑈 2,𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑖𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑒 is the baseline for normalized second-order entropy calculated for each experiment separately by averaging the (normalized) second-order entropy (𝑈 2 ) of 500 random sequences using the exact same block length and number of choice options from each experiment. The measure, 𝑈 2,𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑎𝑟𝑑 , is the final standardized and normalized second-order entropy. This is what we use to compare entropy between experiments, and will be simply called 'entropy' for short.

Reinforcement learning models

Our model is based on a traditional Rescorla-Wagner (RW) model ( 62 Here, 𝑄 stands for Q-value, t is trial, a is action, P is probability, ε is the stochasticity, c the index of the chosen action, r is the reward ∈ {0, 1}, and α is the learning rate.

The stochasticity parameter ε corresponds to a stochastic generator mechanism and the learning rate α to a fast reinforcement learning mechanism. We compared different variations of the model that could include up to three extra free parameters representing the three memory-based mechanisms (23).

The first extension includes an update rule for all unchosen actions and represents the action-frequency-based memory. This is governed by the parameter λ, referred to as the unchosenaction bias. Mathematically, it is implemented by adding λ to the Q-values of all unchosen actions: Here S represents the sequence value. The unchosen-sequence bias λs is added to all unchosen action sequences {𝑎 𝑡-1 , 𝑎 𝑡 }. Infrequent sequences are up valued when λs is positive (beneficial in an adversarial environment) and down valued when λs is negative (beneficial in a stable environment). It thus serves as a memory for how infrequent certain subsequences (consisting of two actions) were made before. When choosing an action, the 𝑄 value of each action and the 𝑆 value of each action given the previous action are integrated in the decision-making policy, by simply adding them:

The third extension was integrated into the decision-making rule, providing the model with a probability to tap into episodic memory. This is modeled using the parameter γ, representing the probability of selecting an action from a buffer of size K, with K being the number of choice alternatives. We created two versions of our models within this first extension containing γ as a free parameter. In the first version, the buffer contains all K most recent chosen actions and γ is denoted as γr (r for recent). In the second version, the buffer contains all actions that are not among the K most recently chosen actions and γ is denoted as γnr (nr for nonrecent). The same amount of information is kept in memory when using either γr or γnr, namely an episode of recent actions.

The difference is whether one samples inside (γr) or outside (γnr) this buffer. The decision-making policy, containing ε and γ is formulated as follows:

Decision at trial 𝑡: { argmax{𝑉 𝑡-1 (𝑎)} with 𝑃 = 1 -𝜀 -𝛾 𝑟 (𝑜𝑟 1 -𝜀 -𝛾 𝑛𝑟 ) random action with 𝑃 = 𝜀 recent (or nonrecent) action with 𝑃 = 𝛾 𝑟 (𝑜𝑟 𝛾 𝑛𝑟 ) where 𝑉 can be a combined Q-value and γ represents episodic memory.

In previous studies, we already confirmed through optimization simulations that upregulating any of these five parameters can lead to more variable choice-making in adversarial environments, with each parameter linked to a different cognitive mechanism (23). The question remains what humans do. To find out, we fitted 18 different versions of the model on the hideand-seek data and evaluated model fits using the BIC criterion. These 18 models all contain at minimum the ε parameter and are then constructed using a full factorial combination of the α, λ and γ parameters, where these are either set to 0 or fitted as a free parameter. The γ parameter can be fitted as either γr or γnr. The λS parameter only occurs in models that already contain λ, representing 6 of the 18 models. A summary of the mechanisms, model equations, parameters and model constructs can be found in Table 1. This allowed us to assess which parameters are useful to adapt between different variability regimes, suggesting the presence of the associated variability source. Note: The models containing episodic memory each have two versions, one with γr and one with γnr, making a total of 18 models.

Simulations, model recovery and parameter recovery

We also investigated the efficiency of these parameters in generating adaptive variability.

We simulated the adversarial environment with values covering the full range of each parameter, while keeping the other four parameters constant, and then calculated the resulting entropy. The constant values of the other parameters were set to the average estimated parameter values when fitting the full ε-α-λ-λS-γnr model on the hide-and-seek data, except for γ which was set to 0 to not favor γr or γnr in these simulations. For ε, we simulated 10 sequences for 101 values of ε in the [0, 1] interval, evenly spaced with jumps of 0.01, and calculated the average entropy for each value.

The same principle was done with α. For λ and λS, we simulated 10 sequences for 100 evenly spaced values of those parameters in the [-0.125, 0.125] interval. Last, for γr and γnr, we simulated 10 sequences for all evenly spaced values within the [0, 1-εav] with steps of 0.01, where εav is the average stochasticity value from the hide-and-seek data. By doing this, we could plot each parameter as a function of entropy and see its effect.

Before fitting the models on the empirical data, we also performed a model recovery. For this, we simulated with each model between 502 and 651 datasets of 800 trials each, including 150 datasets obtained by sampling the estimated parameter sets for the second hide and seek Experiment. The other datasets resulted from random parameter sampling. We also performed a parameter recovery for the full model. For this, we used the same simulated datasets used in the model recovery, comparing for each model the truly used parameters with the estimated parameters after going through our model fitting process. Lastly, to investigate the efficiency of the mechanisms that are present in the empirical data, we analyzed the parameter values of the winning models in each environment. All data and scripts for analyses are publicly available at https://osf.io/hu63g.

References

We performed a parameter recovery for the full ε-α-λ-λS-γnr model, and for the γr parameter in the ε-α-λ-λS-γr model to assess if parameter values can be accurately estimated. The results can be seen in Figure S2.2. The Pearson correlation values of the parameter recovery can be seen in Table S2.1. The results indicate a good identifiability of all parameters (> 84%). Entropy analyses

A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of environment on entropy in Experiment 1 (Figure 1A). Mauchly's test showed a violation of sphericity W = 0.61, p < .001, so a Greenhouse-Geisser correction was used (eps = .72), F(1.44,96.52) = 152.61, p < .001, η² = .69. Post-hoc paired t-tests (Holm-corrected) revealed significantly higher entropy in the adversarial environment than in both the stable environment (p < .001) and volatile environment (p < .001). The entropy in the stable environment was significantly higher than in the volatile environment (p = .017).

In Experiment 2 (Figure 1B), the effect of environment on entropy was again significant, and a Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied (eps = .73) because sphericity was violated (W = 0.63, p < .001), F(1.46, 218.18) = 203.95, p < .001, η² = .58. Holm-corrected paired t-tests indicated that the behavior in the adversarial environment resulted in higher entropy than in both the stable environment (p < .001), and volatile environment (p < .001). The volatile environment resulted in higher choice entropy than the stable environment (p < .001).

Also for Experiment 3, a repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong effect of environment on entropy, with again a violation of sphericity (W = 0.31, p < .001) and a Greenhouse-Geisser correction (eps = .59), F(1.18, 84.13) = 411.74, p < .001, η² = .85. Holm-corrected paired t-tests again revealed that the adversarial environment leads to the highest entropy (p < .001 compared to stable and p < .001 compared to volatile), followed by the volatile and stable environments (p < .001).

In other words, all experiments showed significant differences in entropy across all environments, except when comparing the stable and volatile environments in Experiment 1. This might be due to the design of Experiment 1, where blocks were shorter (200 trials) and the three highly rewarding hiding spots changed between blocks. Similarly, entropy was lower in the stable condition in Experiment 2, but still relatively high, potentially because participants still switched between the three highly rewarding hiding spots. In Experiment 3, only one choice option was highly rewarding (like most stable environments in prior literature), leading to the lowest entropy levels (see Figure 1). Nevertheless, our critical comparison was with the adversarial environment, which always led to significantly higher entropy across experiments.

Model recovery and parameter recovery analyses

We performed a model recovery to evaluate if the correct model (out of 18) can be identified based on the lowest BIC value, given a dataset generated by a known model. The confusion matrix on a group level can be seen in Figure S2.1. This matrix shows the percentage of best model fits on a group level (with groups consisting of 10 datasets) when each simulated model went through our model fitting process. It shows that our models can be well identified in most of the cases (> 78%).

Figure S2.1: Model recovery for the 18 models. Between 502 and 651 datasets were simulated for each model and then fitted on the other models. The matrix shows which model results in the best model fit for groups of 10 datasets.

Model fit based on lowest BIC for each condition and each experiment

All 18 models were fit on each condition in all three experiments (Figure S3.1). The full ε-αλ-λS-γnr model provided the best fit across all environments in Experiments 1 and 2, with an exception in Experiment 2 for the stable environment, where the full ε-α-λ-λS-γr model won. In Experiment 3 (where there were only four response options), the ε-α-λ-λS-γr model gave a better fit in stable and adversarial environments, while the ε-α-λ-γr model fitted best for the volatile environment.

The models are the same as first proposed inReynders et al. (2026). In the traditional RW model, every action (hiding spot) is associated with a Q-value that is updated trial-by-trial governed by a learning rate α. A decision is made by choosing the action with the currently highest Q-value with a probability of 1 -ε, otherwise, a random action is selected. This model is mathematically formulated as: Decision at trial 𝑡: { argmax{𝑄 𝑡-1 (𝑎)} with 𝑃 = 1 -𝜀 random action with 𝑃 = 𝜀 𝑄 𝑡 (𝑎, 𝑐) = 𝑄 𝑡-1 (𝑎, 𝑐) + 𝛼(𝑟 𝑡-1 -𝑄 𝑡-1 (𝑎, 𝑐)) 𝑡 (𝑎, 𝑢) = 𝑄 𝑡-1 (𝑎, 𝑢) + 𝜆 where u stands for unchosen action.

The unchosen-action bias 𝜆 allows to up-value (positive value) or down-value (negative value) unchosen actions. The adding (or subtracting) of λ when an action is not chosen, turns the Q-values into a composite signal of choice (in)frequency of that action (action-frequency-based memory), and the expected long-term rewards based on immediate feedback (reinforcement learning). The second extension represents a sequence-frequency-based memory and adds a learning rule for learning values of sequences of actions. Specifically, the model keeps track of the frequency of certain sequences of actions in a similar way as how λ keeps track of choice infrequency of actions. It is governed by the parameter λs, named the unchosen-sequence bias: 𝑆 𝑡 ({𝑎 𝑡-1 , 𝑎 𝑡 }, 𝑢) = 𝑆 𝑡-1 ({𝑎 𝑡-1 , 𝑎 𝑡 }, 𝑢) + 𝜆 𝑠 a) with P = 1-ε random action with P = ε Vt(a) = Qt(a) + St(a) ε ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Fast reinforcement learning Qt(a,c) = Qt-1(a,c) + α PE PE = rt -Qt-1(a,c) a) with P = 1-ε-γ random action with P = ε (non)recent action with P = γ Vt(a) = Qt(at) + St({at-1,at})
